video.title: You’re Doing Everything Except the One Thing That Works

summary: Chris Koerner and Sam Thompson discuss how to validate business ideas through calls with potential customers and paid tests, rather than extended planning. They use a Google Maps service and Sam’s seasonal hummingbird nectar business to show how conversations can change an offer and pricing. They also explore one-time software templates, AI-generated video ads, and short-form media businesses. The main lesson is to take action, learn from real customers, and give an idea enough time to produce useful results.

speakers.name: Sam Thompson
speakers.description: Discusses his hummingbird nectar business and experiments with AI-generated video.

ideas.name: Google Maps ranking and reputation management service
ideas.one_liner: Sell local businesses help with Google Maps visibility, ranking, and reviews, adjusting the offer to match what owners say they need.
ideas.business_model: Monthly service retainer, potentially supported by white-label software.
ideas.customer: Local business owners who want to rank higher on Google Maps and attract more customers.
ideas.problem: Owners may care more about ranking and getting people through the door than about review management itself.
ideas.offer: A Google Maps ranking audit and help improving visibility; the operator initially considered review management, then changed the ads and offer after customer calls.

pricing.model: Monthly retainer; the operator was advised to discover willingness to pay through sales calls.

price_points.unit: per client, per month, estimated software cost
per month, suggested service price range

pricing.notes: The operator had not settled on pricing. Chris suggested using customer conversations to find a price that fits the customer and the operator's costs.

acquisition_channels.details: The operator ran Facebook ads with a broad message asking whether business owners struggled with Google Maps and inviting them to schedule a call. He later changed the ads to focus on ranking higher.

ideas.delivery: The operator sells and delivers the service himself, using white-label software. Chris says the operator is not hiring anyone and expects to spend time on clients.
unit_economics_claims: The operator booked calls for about $30 each at first and later about $18 each after changing the ad message.
Chris estimated software might cost about $100 per client and suggested a possible selling price of $400–$600 per month.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the operator spent money on Facebook ads.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Chris says the operator had three active clients after about a month; exact time to first payment is not stated.

acquisition.how: Paid social campaigns and call booking can be automated with routine checks, but the described approach depends on a human reviewing results and taking sales calls.

onboarding.how: Forms and software can collect business details, but the operator may need to assess each location and agree on goals.

delivery.how: White-label software may handle some work, but the operator is expected to spend time managing clients and delivering the service.

billing.how: Recurring invoicing can be automated, with a human handling exceptions and pricing decisions.

support.how: Routine questions could use software, but client communication and advice remain human-led in the described model.

uk_applicability.notes: Google Maps and local business search work in the UK. Paid social can reach business owners without unsolicited direct messaging.

risks: The operator had no experience with Google Maps optimisation, so delivery quality and results were not established.
The service may require substantial ongoing client work.
Ad costs, client conversion, and retention may vary.

ideas.name: Hummingbird nectar ecommerce
ideas.one_liner: Sell bagged hummingbird food through online ads, testing pack sizes and bundles around a seasonal buying period.
ideas.business_model: One-off product sales, with possible repeat orders and marketplace sales.
ideas.problem: Customers need nectar for their feeders and may need convenient pack sizes and shipping.
ideas.offer: Bagged hummingbird nectar, with Sam considering smaller bags and a starter pack after finding his initial bags too large and shipping inconvenient.

pricing.model: One-off ecommerce product sales; planned offers were still being tested.
pricing.notes: Sam was still testing pack size and offers. He described the business as seasonal and planned to prepare for Amazon sales the following summer.

acquisition_channels.details: Sam started pushing Facebook ads to the product and said he planned to keep testing offers.
Sam planned to prepare an Amazon launch for the next summer season.

ideas.delivery: Sam buys bags and ingredients, scoops sugar into bags in his garage, and ships product to customers. He had encountered shipping delays and was considering changing pack size.
unit_economics_claims: Sam said his per-bag cost could fall from $8 to $4 with a smaller pack.
Sam said the business had generated thousands of dollars in profit, but did not provide a period or detailed accounting.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Sam says he started the business in a few hours and began selling after running ads; an exact time to first revenue is not stated.

acquisition.how: Paid ads and marketplace listings can run with routine human oversight, while creative and campaign decisions still need review.

onboarding.how: An ecommerce checkout can collect orders and shipping details automatically.

delivery.how: Sam describes physically scooping and packing sugar, handling inventory, and dealing with shipping. Fulfilment would need a human or a contracted warehouse.

billing.how: Marketplace and ecommerce payments can be processed automatically, with human handling for refunds and disputes.

support.how: Order-status questions and common product questions can be templated, but shipping problems and customer complaints require human review.

uk_applicability.notes: Online product sales and Amazon exist in the UK, but hummingbird demand is more seasonal and may differ with UK climate and bird-feeding habits. Food product rules, labelling, and shipping need UK-specific checks.

risks: Sam said the bags took a long time to arrive and that he may have miscalculated the pack size.
He had not worked out the supply chain for a liquid add-on.
The business is seasonal, with Sam describing a three-to-four-month busy period.
Physical packing and fulfilment limit unattended operation unless outsourced.

ideas.name: Hummingbird nectar extender
ideas.one_liner: Sell a small bottle of water and copper sulfate as an add-on intended to help nectar last longer.
ideas.business_model: One-off product sales, sold separately or bundled with hummingbird nectar.
ideas.customer: Hummingbird feeder owners who want nectar to stay usable longer.
ideas.problem: Nectar can go bad while sitting in a feeder.
ideas.offer: A small bottle of water and micronutrient copper sulfate, which Sam described as an antibacterial extender.

pricing.model: One-off sales and a proposed bundle with nectar pouches.
pricing.notes: Sam had not worked out the liquid supply chain or confirmed his planned bundle.

acquisition_channels.details: Sam referred to a competitor selling the extender on Amazon and considered Amazon for his own future sales.
Sam planned to test the product and bundles through his existing Facebook ad approach.

ideas.delivery: The product would need to be mixed, bottled, bundled, and shipped. Sam said he had not worked out how to source and prepare the liquid.
unit_economics_claims: Sam said a competitor's ingredient cost was under $1 per bottle and that the competitor sold about 1,000 units per month.
Sam estimated empty tincture bottles could cost about 30 cents each.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; Sam had not worked out the liquid supply chain.

acquisition.how: Marketplace listings and paid ads can be managed with software and routine human review.

onboarding.how: A standard online checkout can collect orders automatically.

delivery.how: Mixing, bottling, quality checks, and physical shipping require people or a fulfilment partner.

billing.how: Online payments can be processed automatically.

support.how: Routine order support can be templated, but product safety and performance complaints need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: UK ecommerce infrastructure is available, but product safety, chemical handling, labelling, and the size of the hummingbird market would need checking. The bird-feeding use case may be less familiar in the UK.

risks: Sam had not verified the formula, supply chain, or shipping requirements.
A product making claims about keeping nectar fresh could need substantiation and appropriate product labelling.
Physical mixing and bottling are not suitable for unattended delivery.

ideas.name: Customisable personal CRM app built on a coding platform
ideas.one_liner: Offer a ready-made personal CRM with an interface that lets customers request custom features through an AI coding tool.
ideas.business_model: Potential software subscription for customisation, possibly combined with a paid template.
ideas.customer: People who want a personal CRM but do not find existing contact apps or CRMs suitable.
ideas.problem: General-purpose apps may not fit a person's workflow, while software customisation can feel difficult or technical.
ideas.offer: A personal CRM with common features and a chat-based way to request additions such as birthday reminders or dark mode, with a coding platform making changes behind the scenes.

pricing.model: Not settled; the discussion considers a one-time template purchase and a possible recurring fee for customisation.
pricing.notes: The host's initial concept was a white-labelled Replit-style experience; Sam suggested selling a template instead.

acquisition_channels.details: The speakers discuss using Facebook ads to find buyers and learn which features people want; no campaign for this product is described as launched.

ideas.delivery: Software would provide the CRM and route customisation requests to an AI coding platform. Human product decisions and support would still be needed.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers said customisation could use platform credits, but did not establish average credit use or cost for this specific app.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; this was a proposed business.

acquisition.how: Paid ads, a product page, and in-app trial flows can be automated, with human review of campaign performance.

onboarding.how: Account creation and importing contacts could be handled by software, with human support for unusual imports.

delivery.how: An AI coding platform could handle some feature requests, but changes need testing, security review, and approval.

billing.how: Subscription billing can run automatically, with occasional human handling of failed payments and cancellations.

support.how: An agent can answer common questions, but custom software failures and data issues need human escalation.

uk_applicability.notes: A personal CRM can serve UK users, but it would need suitable privacy, security, and UK GDPR practices for contact data.

risks: Users may pay for customisation but rarely use it, leaving the cost of the feature hard to recover.
AI-generated code can introduce defects or data-security issues.
The speakers question whether less technical customers actually want to customise their apps.

tactics.name: Validate by speaking with potential customers before building
steps: Choose a specific customer group and a broad problem area.
Run a simple ad that invites people to schedule a call.
Ask what they are struggling with and use probing questions tied to the area you can serve.
Use the answers to decide what to sell, rather than assuming the first offer is correct.

quote.text: get on sales calls with nothing to sell just ask them what they're struggling with they just tell you the problem
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use ad results to refine the promise
steps: Start with a broad message connected to a clear customer problem.
Book calls and listen for the outcome customers ask for most.
Update the ad and landing page to reflect that outcome.
Compare the cost per booked call before and after the change.

quote.text: So then he changed his ads to speak to that of like we'll help you rank on Google Maps better
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use discovery calls to set an initial price
steps: Know the minimum price that covers software and delivery time.
Ask the prospect what the outcome is worth to them and what they can afford.
Treat early price conversations as customer research.
Record differences between customer types and test price points over more calls.

quote.text: you can AB test pricing live on the phone as long as you know what your floor is especially early
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Use customer language to explain the value
steps: Ask what one customer lead or job is worth in profit.
Estimate the value of the additional leads the service could generate.
Compare that value with the proposed service fee.
State a guarantee only if you can honour it and the terms are clear.

quote.text: so are you telling me that every call you get organically from Google is worth $60 is that accurate
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Get a first customer who does not know you
steps: Use friends and family if they help you learn how to sell and deliver.
Then test whether someone without a personal connection will pay.
Treat a stranger's purchase and feedback as a stronger test of demand than warm support.

quote.text: every business that's going to reach a meaningful size comes from getting people to pay you that do not know you
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Treat a first product offer as a test
steps: Check whether pack size and shipping cost work before scaling inventory.
Test a starter pack and bundle discount.
Track whether buyers repeat orders and whether the bundle raises average order value.
Resolve supply-chain questions before committing to a new liquid product.

quote.text: I think I did my math wrong on the size of the bag that I needed and so I'm going to change my top offunnel offer to sample pack
quote.speaker: Sam Thompson

tactics.name: Use AI video to test creative concepts before hiring a creator
steps: Generate several short versions with different hooks, characters, or scripts.
Run the versions and identify which hook performs best.
Invest in a human creator for the stronger concept.
Check the final video for inaccurate text, odd background details, and character inconsistencies.

quote.text: what we end up doing is we run those and then we say Oh this hook is our highest performer let's go have like an actual UGC creator
quote.speaker: Sam Thompson

tactics.name: Structure a video prompt in layers
steps: Describe the setting and time of day.
Specify the visual style and camera behaviour.
Define each character's appearance and personality.
Write the dialogue and describe how the characters interact.
Remove quotation marks or platform names if they cause unwanted subtitles.

quote.text: most of the time I start with it's like setting right and so like a busy sidewalk in a urban neighborhood at sunset
quote.speaker: Sam Thompson

tactics.name: Commit to a test period before switching ideas
steps: Choose one business idea.
Keep doing the actions that are meant to produce results.
Allow enough time for the test to produce evidence before switching.

quote.text: pick something commit to it for 60 days and just actually do the things that drive results
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Use first-party customer evidence to complement market research, rather than relying only on search trends or an LLM's estimate.

quote.text: first party data run your own ads figure out what your cost per click is do your sales calls figure out the customer's willingness to pay
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: Use real customer conversations to understand willingness to pay, and know your minimum viable price before negotiating.

quote.text: you can AB test pricing live on the phone as long as you know what your floor is especially early
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A stranger buying is a stronger demand signal than a friend buying to support the founder.

quote.text: when you start with a first customer that's a stranger to you it's like a clean slate and it's a perfect case study

lessons.lesson: Take action quickly, then be patient while you learn and wait for results.

quote.text: impatience with action patience with results go launch the thing today but be patient with figuring it all out

lessons.lesson: Practice in the real world can teach faster than extended preparation in a low-stakes setting.

quote.text: over the next 12 weeks you learn 10 times more than what you learned in the previous 12 weeks because you're in the deep end

lessons.lesson: Use customer language and customer outcomes to make an offer easy to understand.
